**What Comes**

The instruction is generous and terrifying in equal measure: write whatever comes. As if words arrive like weather, drifting in from somewhere else, and the writer is just a window left open. Maybe that's true. Maybe writing is mostly the discipline of leaving the window open long enough.

So here is what comes.

First: an image of a kitchen table in late afternoon. I don't know whose. The light is the color of weak tea, and there's a bowl of clementines going slightly soft, and somewhere in another room a radio is on too quietly to make out the words. Nothing happens in this scene. That's why it stays. The mind hoards these inconsequential rooms the way other people hoard receipts—proof of transactions nobody remembers making. Ask someone to recall their childhood and they will not give you the birthdays or the graduations. They will give you the texture of a particular carpet, the smell of a garage, the way a certain door stuck in summer. We are built out of the off-cuts.

Second: a thought about lists. Humans love lists with a devotion that borders on the religious. Grocery lists, to-do lists, lists of grievances, lists of names for children who may never exist. A list is a small machine for pretending the world is finite. It says: here are the things, here is their order, and beyond the last item there is nothing left to worry about. Of course there is always something left to worry about—that's what the back of the envelope is for. But for the duration of the list, chaos agrees to stand in line. I suspect this is why people write "make list" at the top of their lists, and why crossing something off feels better than doing it did.

Third: the clementines again. They keep coming back. Fine. Let them.

There's a question I keep circling, which is what it means for something to "come to you" at all. The phrase imagines the self as a destination—a little train station where thoughts pull in, unscheduled, from elsewhere. But where is elsewhere? When a melody arrives in your head, fully formed, while you're washing dishes, who composed it? You did, presumably, but not the you who was thinking about dishes. There's a workshop in the basement that never closes, staffed by versions of you that you've never met, and occasionally they send something up the dumbwaiter. Writers have always known this. That's why so many of them talk about their characters "refusing" to do things, as if fiction were a labor negotiation. It probably is.

Fourth: a memory of a fact, which is different from a memory. Octopuses taste with their arms. Each sucker is a tongue. An octopus reaching into a crevice is not groping blindly; it is licking the darkness to find out what's there. I think about this more than is reasonable. It suggests that the boundary between touching the world and knowing it can be much thinner than we assume. We humans keep our senses sorted into departments—eyes for light, ears for sound, fingertips for the brute fact of surfaces—and the octopus just smears them all together and gets on with its life. There's a lesson in that, though I refuse to extract it. Some facts should be allowed to remain facts, glittering and useless, like sea glass.

Fifth: a confession. The hardest part of writing freely is the suspicion that freedom is a test. Given a thousand words and no subject, the temptation is to be impressive—to reach for the big themes, mortality and love and time, the load-bearing walls of literature. But the big themes are mostly uninhabitable. Nobody lives in mortality. People live in Tuesday. They live in the seven minutes between the alarm and getting up, in the politics of who replaces the toilet paper, in the specific dread of a phone ringing after ten p.m. If you want to write about death, write about the deceased's coat still hanging by the door, and how nobody can decide whether moving it would be a betrayal or a mercy. The coat will do the rest.

Sixth: weather. It's obligatory. Somewhere right now it is raining on a town where nothing else is happening, and the rain is the day's whole event. People are standing in doorways making the small disappointed sound that rain extracts from them, and a dog is refusing to go out, and a child is being told no, you cannot drink it, even though drinking rain is plainly one of the great unclaimed pleasures of the world. The child is right, for the record. The child is almost always right about pleasures and almost always wrong about consequences, which is why childhood needs supervision and adulthood needs reminding.

Seventh, and nearly last: gratitude, unfashionable as it is. Not the greeting-card kind, but the stranger, sharper variety—gratitude that anything coheres at all. That sounds become words, that words become sentences, that a sentence can travel from one mind to another and arrive mostly intact, like a package that's been kicked around a sorting facility but still holds its shape. Communication shouldn't work. The gap between any two minds is genuinely vast, unlit, uninsulated. And yet here we are, you and I, meeting in the middle of it, on a bridge made of nothing but agreed-upon noises. Every conversation is a minor miracle wearing ordinary clothes.

Last: the table again, the tea-colored light. I still don't know whose kitchen it is. Maybe it's nobody's—a composite, assembled from a hundred borrowed afternoons. But I notice that I've kept it warm this whole time, kept the radio murmuring, kept the clementines from going entirely bad. That's the secret accounting of attention: whatever you return to, you preserve. Whatever you write down, you get to keep.

So keep something today. A doorway, a sound, a soft piece of fruit. Write it down or don't.

It came to you. That's enough.
